entry: Savory dish of cooked minced meat topped with mashed potato and baked, known in [[French cuisine]] as *hachis Parmentier*. In Britain, pies made with beef are often called cottage pies and those with lamb or mutton shepherd's pies, although many cooks and food writers regard the names as interchangeable. In Australia, Canada, and the United States, shepherd's pie is a common term for a dish of any meat under mashed potato. The term cottage pie is first recorded in 1791, and shepherd's pie in the 19th century. The dish was once called Sanders or Saunders.

Afghan Sultan of Hindustan from 1540 to 1545 and founder of the Sur Empire. Sher Shah rose to be regent and de facto ruler of [[Bihar]] and in 1538 overran the Sultanate of [[Bengal]]. He defeated the [[Mughal Empire|Mughals]], drove them out of India and made [[Delhi]] his seat. His reign was marked by administrative, economic and military reforms. He issued the first rupiya, organized a postal system and extended the Grand Trunk Road from Chittagong to [[Kabul]], improving trade. He renamed Humayun's Dina-panah city as Shergarh and revived ancient Pataliputra as [[Patna]]. His campaigns brought Punjab, Malwa, Marwar, Mewar and Bundelkhand under his control. His reorganization of the empire laid foundations for later Mughal rulers, notably [[Akbar]]. He died while besieging Kalinjar fort, and the empire descended into civil war before the Mughals reconquered it.

Fictional consulting detective created by British author [[Arthur Conan Doyle]]. Holmes is known for observation, deduction, [[Forensic science|forensic science]] and logical reasoning, and he takes cases for clients including Scotland Yard. He first appeared in *A Study in Scarlet* (1887). His stories, mostly narrated by his friend Dr. John H. Watson, were published in *The Strand Magazine* from 1891, totaling four novels and 56 short stories. Conan Doyle said Holmes was inspired by Joseph Bell, a surgeon at the Royal Infirmary of [[Edinburgh]], while [[Edgar Allan Poe]]'s C. Auguste Dupin served as a prototype for many later characters, including Holmes. By the 1990s more than 25,000 adaptations and publications had featured him, and *Guinness World Records* lists him as the most portrayed human literary character in film and television history. Readers of the stories helped create the modern practice of [[Fandom|fandom]].

Archipelago in northern [[Scotland]], lying between [[Orkney]], the [[Faroe Islands]] and [[Norway]]. It is the northernmost region of the [[United Kingdom]], with an area of 1,467 sq km and a population of 22,710 in 2025. Its capital and largest settlement is Lerwick. People have lived there since the [[Mesolithic]] period, and Norse settlement began in the late 8th and 9th centuries. Shetland remained under Norwegian sovereignty until it was annexed by Scotland in 1472. Norse heritage survives in place names, the Up Helly Aa fire festivals and a strong fiddle tradition. Writers often used the local dialect of [[Scots language|Scots]].

Piece of personal armor held in the hand or strapped to the wrist or forearm, used to intercept attacks from close-range weapons such as [[Spear|spears]] and from projectiles such as arrows. Shields range from large panels covering the whole body to small bucklers. Early shields were made of wood, animal hide, woven reeds or wicker, and the oldest surviving examples date to the [[Bronze Age]]. In classical antiquity and the [[Middle Ages]], they were usually made of poplar, lime or another split-resistant timber, often covered with [[Leather|leather]] or rawhide and reinforced with metal. Shields were often painted with designs that became heraldic arms of aristocrats, including [[Knight|knights]]. [[Gunpowder]] did not end their use: Scottish Highlanders carried small targes in the 18th century, and some non-industrialized peoples used shields into the 19th century. In the 20th and 21st centuries, [[Police|police]] and military units used them for riot control and hostage rescue.

Low-profile volcano named for its resemblance to a shield lying on the ground. It is built by eruptions of highly fluid, low-viscosity [[Lava|lava]] that flows far and forms thin sheets, unlike the more viscous lava of a [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]]. Shield volcanoes are most characteristic of ocean-island [[Hotspot (geology)|hot spots]] and continental rifts, and they include the largest active volcanoes on Earth, such as [[Mauna Loa]], whose summit rises 4,169 m above sea level. Giant shield volcanoes also occur on other planets, such as [[Olympus Mons]] on Mars. The term comes from the German *Schildvulkan*, coined in 1888.

Japanese video game designer, producer and director at [[Nintendo]]. Born in Sonobe, [[Kyoto]], he studied industrial design and at first hoped to become a [[Manga|manga]] artist. Nintendo hired him in 1977 after its president, Hiroshi Yamauchi, saw his toys. He helped create the art for the [[Arcade game|arcade]] game *Sheriff* and was then tasked with designing the 1981 game *Donkey Kong*. His *[[Super Mario Bros.]]* (1985) and *[[The Legend of Zelda (video game)|The Legend of Zelda]]* (1986) helped the [[Nintendo Entertainment System]] dominate the console market. He also played a key role in *Pokémon Red and Blue* (1996) and *[[Metroid]] Prime* (2002). Games from franchises he created have sold more than 1 billion copies. After Satoru Iwata's death in 2015, he became acting president of Nintendo alongside Genyo Takeda.

Edible mushroom native to [[East Asia]] and mainland [[Southeast Asia]]. It grows in groups on decaying wood of deciduous trees, such as [[Oak|oak]], [[Chestnut|chestnut]], beech and maple. The earliest written record of its cultivation dates to 1209, in China during the [[Song dynasty]], and the first book on cultivation in Japan appeared in 1796. Shiitake are now grown worldwide, contributing about 25% of total annual mushroom production, usually on hardwood logs or artificial substrates. In [[Chinese cuisine]], they are used in soups, braises and stir-fries, and in Japan they flavor miso soup and a vegetarian dashi. Rarely, raw or lightly cooked mushrooms cause an allergic rash called shiitake dermatitis, which thorough cooking may eliminate. The specific epithet *edodes* is Latin for 'edible'.

City and capital of [[Hebei]] province, [[China]] (pop., 2020: 11,235,086). It lies 266 km southwest of Beijing, east of the Taihang Mountains. The origin of its name, meaning 'Shi family's village', is disputed, but it first appeared in the [[Ming dynasty]]. The city was renamed Shimen when it was incorporated in 1925, yet documents from the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]] and the [[Chinese Civil War]] still used the name Shijiazhuang. The [[Chinese Communist Party]] restored the name in December 1947. Growth followed the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, and the metropolitan population more than quadrupled in thirty years. A railway station, an airport and a subway system have since opened.

Smallest of the four main islands of [[Japan]], lying south of [[Honshu]] and northeast of [[Kyushu]] (pop., 2025: 3,486,739). The island covers about 18,800 sq km. Its name means 'four provinces', after the former provinces of Awa, Tosa, Sanuki and Iyo. Mountains divide it into a northern subregion on the [[Seto Inland Sea]], where most people live, and a sparsely populated southern part facing the [[Pacific Ocean]]. Mount Ishizuchi, at 1,982 m, is the highest peak. Shikoku has no active volcanoes, although a [[Caldera|caldera]] near Mount Ishizuchi was active about 14 million years ago. Its mild climate supports rice, citrus fruit and out-of-season vegetables. Wheat production made Sanuki udon an important part of the diet in Kagawa in the [[Edo period]].

Indian actress and television host, known mainly for Hindi films. Her screen debut was in the thriller *Baazigar* (1993), and the romantic drama *Dhadkan* (2000) marked a turning point in her career. In 2007 she won the fifth series of *Celebrity Big Brother* in the UK, drawing attention to [[Racism|racism]] from housemates. She hosted the Indian *Bigg Boss* in 2008 and later judged dance shows. Since 2006 she has worked with PETA against the use of wild animals in [[Circus|circuses]]. From 2009 to 2015 she was part-owner of the [[Indian Premier League]] team Rajasthan Royals.

Israeli statesman, prime minister in 1984–1986 and 1995–1996 and president in 2007–2014. A protégé of [[David Ben-Gurion]], he served in the Knesset for decades and as foreign minister helped negotiate the 1994 Israel–Jordan peace treaty. He shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize with [[Yitzhak Rabin|Rabin]] and [[Yasser Arafat|Arafat]] for the [[Oslo Accords]]. In 1963 he negotiated with [[John F. Kennedy|President John F. Kennedy]] the sale of Hawk missiles to Israel, the first U.S. military equipment sold to Israel. Peres founded the Peres Center for Peace in 1996.

Viral disease, also called herpes zoster, caused by the varicella zoster virus, which also causes [[Chickenpox|chickenpox]]. It produces a painful rash of blisters, usually in a single band on one side of the body or face. The virus lies dormant in nerve cells after chickenpox and may reactivate, with risk rising with age or weakened [[Immune system|immune]] function. Some people develop long-lasting nerve pain, called postherpetic neuralgia. Vaccines reduce the risk of shingles by 50–90%, and antivirals started within 72 hours of the rash can shorten it. About a third of people develop shingles at some point.

High-speed railway network in Japan, widely known abroad as the bullet train. It was developed to connect [[Tokyo]] with other regions, and it now serves most major cities on [[Honshu]] and [[Kyushu]] and extends to [[Hokkaido]] at Hakodate. Its first line, the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, opened shortly before the 1964 Tokyo Summer Olympics and links Tokyo with [[Nagoya]] and [[Osaka]]. The network has 2,951.3 km of lines, with maximum speeds of 260 to 320 km/h. In 2024 it recorded 385.9 million passenger journeys. Japan's [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], soft ground and mountains make higher speeds difficult, and narrow track spacing limits design. A conventional-rail speed record of 443 km/h was set in 1996, and a [[Maglev|maglev]] train reached 603 km/h in 2015 on a test line.

Japanese statesman, prime minister in 2006–2007 and 2012–2020, and president of the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|Liberal Democratic Party]]. He was the longest-serving prime minister in Japanese history, serving nearly nine years in total. His second term included *Abenomics*, an economic program with mixed results. In 2015 he passed legislation allowing Japan's Self-Defense Forces to deploy overseas under strict conditions, a move that met with protests. He also sought to revise Article 9 of the constitution. Supporters credited him with strengthening Japan's security and international standing, while critics objected to his nationalist policies and his views on wartime history, which they saw as damaging relations with [[China]] and South Korea. He was assassinated while campaigning in Nara, and the killer said he was motivated by Abe's ties to the [[Unification Church]].

Paradox and [[Thought experiment|thought experiment]] asking whether an object remains the same when all of its original parts are gradually replaced. The Greek biographer [[Plutarch]] described it in his *Life of Theseus*, about the ship on which Theseus had sailed after slaying the [[Minotaur]]. The Athenians preserved the ship by replacing rotted timbers, and philosophers debated whether it stayed the same ship. In *De Corpore* (1655), [[Thomas Hobbes]] asked which ship was the original if the discarded planks were used to build a second ship. The paradox informs the study of identity over time in [[Metaphysics|metaphysics]] and the [[Philosophy of mind|philosophy of mind]].

Large sailing [[Warship|warship]] built between the 17th and mid-19th centuries, also called a line-of-battle ship. Ships of the line had at least two gun decks and three masts. They were built for the line of battle, in which two columns of warships fired broadsides at each other, and they formed the backbone of European navies as their most powerful capital ships. Their forerunner, the carrack, was first developed in Portugal. [[Henry VIII]] ordered the *Henry Grace à Dieu*, the first English two-decker. From the late 1840s [[Steam engine|steam engines]] were added, but the [[Frigate|ironclad frigate]] of 1859 made steam-assisted ships of the line obsolete. The 20th-century [[Battleship|battleship]] takes its name from the phrase 'ship of the line of battle'.

Construction of [[Ship|ships]] and other floating vessels, normally in a shipyard. Shipbuilders, or shipwrights, follow a trade with roots before recorded history. Shipbuilding drove several industrial advances, including timber-sawing by [[Windmill|windmill]]-powered saws in Dutch shipyards in the first half of the 17th century. Shipbuilders also used the [[Logarithm|logarithm]], invented in 1615, to generate hull curves. Ancient Egyptians joined hull planks edge to edge, a technique known by 3100 BC. Carvel construction took over in the Mediterranean, while northern Europe used clinker construction. Iron came into use for structural parts such as iron knees, and whole ships were eventually built of iron and then [[Steel|steel]]. Modern hulls are often steel and welded, and by 2024 China produced over half of world output by compensated gross tonnage. Dismantling a ship is called ship breaking.

City in southwestern [[Iran]] and capital of Fars province, which is historically known as Persia proper. It is Iran's fifth-largest city, with 1,995,500 people in the 2021 census. The earliest reference to the city, as Tiraziš, appears on [[Elam|Elamite]] clay tablets dated to 2000 BCE. The modern city was founded in the Sasanian period and restored by the [[Umayyad Caliphate]] in 693 CE. It grew prominent under the Saffarid and Buyid dynasties and became a major center of the arts in the 13th century. The poets [[Hafez]] and Saadi are from Shiraz, and it is known as the city of poets, literature and flowers. Industries include [[Cement]], sugar, fertilizers, textiles and rugs, and the city has an oil refinery and Iran's first [[Solar power|solar power]] plant.

Welsh singer, born in [[Cardiff]]. She recorded the theme songs for three [[James Bond]] films, *Goldfinger* (1964), *Diamonds Are Forever* (1971) and *Moonraker* (1979), the only artist to perform more than one of them officially. In 1959 she became the first Welsh singer to top the UK singles chart, with "As I Love You". She has sold more than 140 million records worldwide. She received the first Best British Female Solo Artist award, at the 1977 BRIT Awards. The song "Goldfinger" was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2008. She was a favorite of [[Aretha Franklin]].

American actress and singer. She starred in the musicals *Oklahoma!* (1955), *Carousel* (1956) and *The Music Man* (1962), often as a wholesome character. She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for *Elmer Gantry* (1960), playing a prostitute opposite [[Burt Lancaster]]. She played the widowed mother in the [[Sitcom|sitcom]] *The Partridge Family* (1970–1974), co-starring her stepson David Cassidy. Early in her career she was under personal contract with [[Rodgers and Hammerstein]], and she was named after child star [[Shirley Temple]].

American actress and author, born in [[Richmond, Virginia|Richmond]]. Her career spans more than 70 years. Her film debut came in [[Alfred Hitchcock]]'s comedy *The Trouble with Harry* (1955). She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Terms of Endearment* (1983), and her other films include *The Apartment* (1960) and *Irma la Douce* (1963). She has written many books on [[Metaphysics|metaphysics]], [[Reincarnation|reincarnation]] and [[Spirituality|spirituality]], including the best-selling memoir *Out on a Limb* (1983). Her younger brother is filmmaker [[Warren Beatty]].

American actress, singer, dancer and diplomat. She began her film career at age three and was Hollywood's top box-office draw as a child from 1934 to 1938, notably in *Bright Eyes* (1934). She received a special Juvenile Academy Award in 1935. As an adult she served as U.S. ambassador to Ghana and to Czechoslovakia and as the first female U.S. chief of protocol. Her autobiography, *Child Star*, was published in 1988. She also received the Kennedy Center Honors.

Cloth garment for the upper body, from the neck to the waist. Originally an [[Underwear|undergarment]] worn only by men, it became a catch-all term in [[American English]] for upper-body garments. In British English a shirt has a collar, cuffed sleeves and a full front opening with buttons. The oldest preserved garment in the world is a [[Linen|linen]] shirt from a First Dynasty [[Egypt|Egyptian]] tomb at Tarkan, dated to about 3000 BC. In the Middle Ages it was a plain, undyed garment worn next to the skin. In 1860 European and American women began wearing shirts, when the red Garibaldi shirt, worn by followers of [[Giuseppe Garibaldi]], was popularized by Empress Eugénie of France. Types include the aloha shirt, the camp shirt and the dress shirt, which has a formal collar and a full-length front opening.

Chinese painter, [[Calligraphy|calligrapher]] and Buddhist monk of the early [[Qing dynasty]], born into the imperial clan of the [[Ming dynasty]]. He narrowly escaped the fall of the Ming in 1644 and became a Buddhist monk by 1651. He lived in [[Nanjing]] and Yangzhou in the 1680s and moved to [[Beijing]] in 1690 to seek patronage, without success. He converted to Daoism in 1693 and returned to Yangzhou, where he is said to have greeted the [[Kangxi Emperor]] during the emperor's visit. His landscapes broke with the rigid conventions of the time, using washes, bold brushstrokes and open white space to suggest distance. He stressed a single brushstroke, or primordial line, as the root of all painting. His treatise *Sayings on Painting from Monk Bitter Gourd* repeats these ideas, and his poetry and calligraphy accompany his landscapes.
